One of the most important things any real character in my book has is a voice. Like, I can *hear* them speaking, and if I were better at voice work, I could reproduce it. Side characters take longer to get those voices, but the more lines they speak, the stronger they become. 

Like, the cult leader, Lady Orleans. Her voice is very soft, in a very high register, and comes almost exclusively from the front of the mouth. She speaks slowly, and every word is precisely enunciated, but her tone has just the slightest curve of a smile on the back end, like everything amuses her. Even when she's being very serious, there's a hint of irreverence in her voice. 

On the other end is the actual villain of the whole world, Bloody Bana. She's only got a cameo in this book, but I've known her voice for years. It's brassy, she speaks mostly from the back of the jaw (but not quite all the way in the throat). She draaaaws out a lot of words, and puts a fair bit of vocal fry on certain sounds (like the "Ls" in "well"). Her pitch and cadence are highly variable from one word to the next, and she puts the emphasis on all the wrong words in a sentence. Combine that with her habit of using odd, anachronistic phrasing and her general lack of give-a-fuck, and any conversation with her has someone coming away with a feeling of uncanny valley *wrongness*.

It's kind of moot, because the only things Manufacturing allows you to make that exist in Guildhall at all (as per the most recent item guide, which the core rules refer us to when we go to look it up) are watercraft (row boat, sail boat, raft, canoe, etc.). None of which will come up in-game (in Live, anyway). 

There's also a flying broom, which probably doesn't exist in Guildhall because I feel like we'd have seen them all over already if something that cool was allowed. Oh, hey, and a chariot! I forgot about those. 

So unless you want to RP as a shipwright, there's no practical reason to go above Fashioning III before you've got so much status that it's burning a hole in your pocket. The highest-rank buttons are at III, and the only Guildhall-existent items you can craft with IV and V are as follows:

__Fashioning IV__
Unbreakable Rope
Unbreakable Container
Unbreakable Door
2H Crossbow [Specialty]

__Fashioning V__
Impervious Rope
Impervious Container
Impervious Door
Catapult

Everything else is guns, vehicles, high-tech compound bows, cannons, missile launches, etc. 

There's a *whole bunch* of Artisan exclusive lore that can't really be used much or at all in Guildhall. I find more every time I dig into our charts. 

It feels kind of like the class concept as described by their abilities didn't fully fit in to the high fantasy realm, so a lot of their abilities are just kind of... dangling there. 

Artisans *really* need a lot of love. Whole categories of our lore can't be used, we get the second-lowest number of Rank 5 skills, and get no rank 6 skills at all. The weapon upgrades are situational and expensive. While people are fretting over which runes to choose or what potions to buy, most people can only use one or two of our buttons at all. 

And even then, they're adding, for example, 10 feet to a single knockback sometime in the next 12 hours, for 2 silver (at cost). Or for 3 silver, they can prevent exactly 1 (one) single attack (usually 1 point) of break damage to their weapon. 

That's a *really* hard sell if we're expecting to actually make a profit like the Alchemists can. The most useful, cost-effective thing we can make is the rank I button that cancels a single use of Open Hands. 

Everything else is adding +1 damage one time to one attack, increasing unconsciousness time once for one attack (which sounds great until you realize that most of the time you only need them to be unconscious long enough to fatal finish them), draining stamina once (pointless; bad guys have buckets of stamina, which refreshes when they respawn), and making a weapon survive being accidentally dropped into lava. 

That last one at least has *some* utility, in the rare occasion when lava is a threat, but I honestly believe this was a textual oversight rather than an intended interaction just based on how many people have vehemently argued with me that the buoyancy compensator doesn't actually work that way (even though that's what the explicit text in the book says). 

Anyway, I'm just kind of sad about Artisans right now, especially since Alchemists are I guess about to get transformation lore that isn't even currently in the book before Artisans get to use things that have been in the book for years but that can't be used in Guildhall. 

I guess on the upside, nobody's held Artisan lore hostage against a bonkers plot choice no reasonable person would ever make (hi, Runecasters!). :rofl:

Fall triggers massive stress vibes in me, even though I no longer have to stress about any of it. As soon as the soy starts to turn and the crickets start to chirp, my brain is tracking hay prices, looking for backup suppliers, trying to source good second-cutting bales to fill the loft with. 

I'm looking into firewood suppliers, because the guy I used last year doesn't exist anymore (they never do); guys who can deliver a reasonable quantity of good wood (god, that one guy who tried to mix cottonwood into his cords is *still* on my shitlist) at a reasonable price consistently. Then I need to find a backup guy for when I'm down to my last half-cord and find out the first guy is on vacation in Florida for two weeks. 

I'm harvesting and canning an absolute boatload of tomatoes, spending all day in front of a hot stove cranking that Victorio strainer while watching the pressure gauge on the canner from across the kitchen as the kids just keep bringing in basket after basket. 

I'm weather-proofing the barn, coordinating buck shed time with each of the momma goats who aren't scheduled to milk through, putting out mouse/rat prevention, mowing down the garden, and rushing to do the last few fence repairs before the first snow comes in. 

Then winter is worse. Waking up every 4 hours all night long to keep the wood stove burning (because the model we got didn't have an 8-hour firebox *and let me tell you all about whose fault that was because it sure as fuck wasn't mine*), hauling wood, splitting wood, hauling hay from the loft to the barn, hauling water in buckets from the kitchen to the trough (because the water line from the house to the barn never got fixed *and let me tell you all about whose fault that was...*) through foot-deep snow in steel toed boots because they're the only footwear I own.  

Meanwhile, I'm also nervously sweating as the first cutting hay bales run out, then the second cutting, then the third cutting, and the horses and goats are down to fourth cutting, which is basically just a step up from straw, and praying that the weather doesn't delay next year's first cutting because that's *always* a disaster for hay prices...

Oh, and I'm constantly monitoring the wind direction, every day. If it's coming out of the north, the barn is going to be extra cold if I don't adjust which doors are open. If it's coming out of the west, everything's fine. If it's coming out of the south, the barn is going to be extra cold if don't change the doors from the "north" position to the "south" position, **and** the master bedroom is going to be absolutely freezing because the outside door wasn't installed properly (*and let me tell you all about whose fault that was...*). If it's coming out of the east, the pipes will probably freeze overnight so I need to keep the bottle torch handy. 

Then spring comes, and it gets a little better, but it still sucks, and it's going to suck until Mother's Day, when I can usually start buttoning up the wood stove since we won't (shouldn't) have any more frost. But I can't *completely* shut it down until at least Memorial Day, because nights can still get cold, so now I'm running it low and building up creosote in the chimney, which I have to keep an eye on and always think about. 

Finally, Memorial Day comes, and I can kind of breathe easier because the first cutting of hay is coming down and as long as it doesn't rain much in the next couple days, it'll start getting baled up and my hungry animals can have *real* nutrition again instead of old, stiff, yellowed, mixed-timothy-grass from last year. 

After Memorial Day, things start to look up. 

That's why I prefer summer. Summer is about 85% less stress.

The root of the thing is, I guess, that when I read (and when I write), I expect worlds to get more and more complicated the deeper I look at them. I expect to find more things and make more connections and get a higher and higher resolution as I continue to explore. When I look at the grass, I see dirt; when I look at the dirt, I find worms and rocks, and can use all of that to extrapolate how other places in the same world will function and predict events the way a native of the world could predict events. 

I get frustrated with worlds where looking deeper results in *less* complication. I look at the grass and see brown pixels and texture shaders meant to represent dirt, and a white out-of-bounds void underneath that. There's nothing further to put together; everything on the surface is all there is. Places where I can see the hand of the author or the ticking of the metamechanical clockwork bother me. Which, admittedly, is almost all video games and tabletop games. The lore exists just enough to give the players something to look at while they pass through to the next quest. 

Especially since I don't personally think I'm digging *all that* deep to begin with. I'm just trying to dig deep enough that I could write a short story in the world without mentioning a game mechanic or having to make up important things (like the name of a major non-capital city in the highly urbanized kingdom of Coventry).

Which is what I go for when I'm narratively building a world. There need to be enough details that a person can go in and write a whole new story in that world that's faithful to the setting without needing me (the original author) to micromanage it. 

The more different stories that can be told in a world, and the more different characters can fit into the world, the better the world is built. 

It's possible to have "too many details" if all you're interested in is telling a single story from a single perspective about a single event or sequence of events. If you want a world to be able to hold a dozen different stories or a dozen different characters who never directly influence each other, there's almost no such thing as "too many details" on the page.

Hot take: as an editor, I strongly prefer neopronouns to noun-self pronouns or even the singular "they". Singular "they" creates a lot of vague pronoun reference errors, especially in scenes with two or more characters who use the "they" pronoun. It's much easier to differentiate the actions of an individual from the actions of the group if even one character is using a neopronoun instead.
